issues.legal_issue: A grant to enter land and catch and carry away fish from specified waters is a profit a prendre and immovable property, rather than a sale of future movable goods.
material_facts: The purchasers obtained oral grants for payment permitting them to enter specified sections of a lake and catch and carry away fish during future periods.
The grants concerned the use of a fishery connected with land.
issues.conclusion: The rights granted were profits a prendre and therefore benefits arising out of land and immovable property, not sales of future fish.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(26) of the General Clauses Act, immovable property includes benefits arising out of land. The Transfer of Property Act excludes standing timber, growing crops and grass from its meaning of immovable property, but fish do not fall within those exclusions. The court distinguished Firm Chhotabhai Jethabai Patel & Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, where the right to pluck leaves concerned growing crops.

predicates.grant_allows_entry_onto_land: The grant permits its holder to enter land.
predicates.grant_allows_taking_natural_produce_from: The grant permits its holder to take natural produce from the land.

issues.definition: When a grant permits entry onto land and the taking of natural produce from it, the right is a profit a prendre and immovable property.

issues.legal_issue: An oral sale of an immovable fishery right for a price, without the required written and registered instrument, transfers no title or interest.
material_facts: The fishery rights were granted orally in exchange for payment.
The value of the transactions exceeded the applicable registration threshold.
No written or registered instrument was executed.
issues.conclusion: The transactions did not pass any title or interest to the purchasers.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act requires a sale of immovable property for a price to be made by a written and registered instrument when the property is tangible and exceeds the prescribed value; a registered instrument is required for intangible immovable property regardless of value. Because a profit a prendre is immovable property and the transactions were oral, no title or interest passed.

predicates.immovable_property_is_sold_for_a_price: A transferor purports to sell immovable property in exchange for a price.
predicates.transfer_is_oral: The purported transfer is made orally and no written instrument is executed.
predicates.value_exceeds_registration_threshold: The value of the transferred property exceeds the threshold at which a written and registered instrument is required.

issues.definition: A purported oral sale for a price of immovable property above the registration threshold passes no title or interest.

issues.legal_issue: The State's mere refusal to recognize a contract does not infringe fundamental rights when it neither takes the contract nor claims its benefits, and an ineffective transfer gives the claimants no enforceable property right.
material_facts: The claim was brought to enforce fundamental rights.
The purported fishery transfers were oral and did not pass title or interest.
The State refused to recognize the contracts and was preparing to auction the fishery rights again.
The State did not take possession of the contracts or claim the payments or other benefits under them.
issues.conclusion: The State's refusal to recognize the contracts did not violate the asserted fundamental rights, and the petition was dismissed; any remedy for breach of contract lay, if available, in a civil action.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31(1) of the Constitution, a fundamental-rights claim requires a relevant property interest and State action taking or interfering with it in the manner alleged. The court held that the invalid transfers conferred no enforceable interest. It further held that, even assuming a contract could be property, mere refusal to recognize it was not confiscation, acquisition or taking possession of it; a contractual remedy might instead be pursued by suit.

rule.if: constitutional_enforcement_petition and (transfer_formality_unsatisfied or (contract_assumed_property and state_only_declined_recognition and state_neither_took_contract_nor_claimed_benefits))

predicates.constitutional_enforcement_petition: A claimant seeks relief for an alleged infringement of fundamental rights in a constitutional enforcement proceeding.
predicates.transfer_formality_unsatisfied: The purported transfer was oral and lacked the written and registered instrument required for that transfer.
predicates.contract_assumed_property: The claimant's contract is treated, for purposes of the alternative analysis, as property.
predicates.state_only_declined_recognition: The State refused to recognize the contract and did not assume its obligations.
predicates.state_neither_took_contract_nor_claimed_: The State did not take possession of the contract or claim benefits paid or due under it.

issues.definition: In a constitutional enforcement proceeding, no fundamental-rights violation follows if the transfer lacked required formalities or, even treating the contract as property, the State only declined to recognize it and neither took it nor claimed its benefits.
